extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of literary fiction; students of prose and narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted material pertains to narrative- and rhetoric-level guidance and evaluative rules embedded in an 18th-century comic novel (Tristram Shandy). It includes explicit maxims for judging disputed notions, comments on sermon-writing and dramatick style, and meta-advice for writers about maintaining connection and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate disputed notions by tracing consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The surest way to try the merit of any disputed notion is, to trace down the consequences such a notion has produced, and compare them with the spirit of Christianity;——'tis the short and decisive rule which our Saviour hath left us, for these and such like cases, and it is worth a thousand arguments——By their fruits ye shall know them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consequences/real-world effects of a notion as the decisive test of its merit; compare those consequences to the relevant ethical/spiritual standard (here phrased as 'the spirit of Christianity'). This is presented as a short, decisive rule preferred to lengthy argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspect passion, not reason, in loud attacks on religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a man talks loudly against religion, always suspect that it is not his reason, but his passions, which have got the better of his creed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating rhetorical or polemical assertions (especially strong denunciations), consider emotional motive as the primary cause rather than rational conviction; treat loudness as a heuristic for passion-driven argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret 'against conscience' as physical appetite in such claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When a man, thus represented, tells you in any particular instance,——That such a thing goes 'against his conscience,——always believe he means exactly the same thing, as when he tells you such a thing goes _against_ his stomach;—a present want of appetite being generally the true cause of both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read claims that something is 'against conscience' with skepticism: the text advises treating them as analogous to transient physical aversion (e.g., lack of appetite), implying such claims often reflect immediate personal discomfort rather than principled moral opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust no one lacking conscience across matters
rubrics_metrics.description: In a word,—trust that man in nothing, who has not a CONSCIENCE in every thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A moral-evaluative maxim: consistency of conscience across contexts is a necessary condition for trustworthiness. Use this as a criterion when judging character or testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience is not a law; distinguish judge from lawgiver
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember this plain distinction, a mistake in which has ruined thousands,—that your conscience is not a law;—No, God and reason made the law, and have placed conscience within you to determine;——not, like an _Asiatic_ Cadi, according to the ebbs and flows of his own passions,—but like a _British_ judge..., who makes no new law, but faithfully declares that law which he knows already written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating moral reasoning (or advising others), distinguish between internal conscience (a decision guide) and external law (principles grounded in reason/divine will). Warns against treating shifting personal feelings as law-making authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writers must 'look before them' to preserve spirit and connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers had need look before them, to keep up the spirit and connection of what they have in hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A direct writing guideline: authors should plan or at least be mindful of earlier and later material to maintain coherence of tone, spirit, and narrative connection. The narrator even delays telling certain matters until the place where they will be most advantageous, illustrating deliberate placement for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatick (theatrical) mode of writing catches attention when skilful
rubrics_metrics.description: ’tis dramatick,—and there is something in that way of writing, when skilfully managed, which catches the attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dramatick/scene-based techniques (introducing characters, vivid posture, dialogue, staged description) to engage readers — but emphasize 'skilfully managed' (technique and restraint matter). The narrator compares sermons with dramatick writing as an attention-grabbing model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sermons' stylistic constraint: avoid low characters in pulpit compositions
rubrics_metrics.description: In this, added Dr. _Slop_, a little piqued,—our sermons have greatly the advantage, that we never introduce any character into them below a patriarch or a patriarch’s wife, or a martyr or a saint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a stated stylistic convention (here for sermons), avoid minor or ignoble characters in formal moral/religious expositions; keep figures elevated. The narrator however questions or nuances strict reliance on such constraints elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing and small circumstances alter perception and value
rubrics_metrics.description: Matters of no more seeming consequence in themselves than, 'Whether my father should have taken off his wig with his right hand or with his left,'—have divided the greatest kingdoms... the circumstances with which every thing in this world is begirt, give every thing in this world its size and shape!—and by tightening it, or relaxing it, this way or that, make the thing to be, what it is—great—little—good—bad—indifferent or not indifferent, just as the case happens?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A composition and rhetorical principle: small changes in emphasis, framing, or manner can radically change how an action or passage is judged. Use adjustment of circumstances, timing, or emphasis to alter reader perception and the 'size' of a scene or claim.
